newsitem.title: CHINA: China ponders history and holidays as HK returns.
newsitem.headline: China ponders history and holidays as HK returns.

text.p: For some in Beijing, the return of Hong Kong on July 1 will be a moment of national pride and a chance to ponder the lessons of China's past humiliation at the hands of British imperial might.
For others, Monday's midnight handover of sovereignty will bring little more than a welcome day off from the daily grind.

Many weekend visitors to Beijing's Old Summer Palace, a former pleasure-ground of Chinese emperors that was destroyed by British and French troops in 1860, saw historical lessons in the scenic ruins preserved in what is now a public park.
"The imperial powers burnt the Summer Palace... and stole our territory," said Zhao Chengyu, a 68-year-old retired doctor visiting the park in a state-organised group.
"Now China is strong, so we are getting Hong Kong back," Zhao said.

London seized Hong Kong island as the victory spoils of its victorious 1840-42 Opium War against China's decaying Qing dynasty (1644-1911), a campaign that began more than a century of colonial humiliation for the world's most populous nation.

The Old Summer Palace, much of which was built in Western style by Jesuits at the 18th century court of the Emperor Qianlong, was burned by British soldiers in an 1860 campaign that added the Kowloon peninsula to Britain's Hong Kong territory.

"This is history that cannot be forgotten," said atomic scientist Zheng Zhichu, 58, gazing at a Communist Party-funded memorial emblazoned with the texts of humiliating 19th century "unequal treaties" forced on Beijing by foreign powers.
Zheng said he usually practised traditional Chinese martial arts in another part of the sprawling park but had been drawn to the Western-style ruins by thoughts of the Hong Kong handover.

"The return of Hong Kong is a great thing for the Chinese people," he said, adding that he held no hard feelings against the British, who had turned their colony from a sleepy island into a major metropolis.
"Britain very peacefully returned Hong Kong to us -- that is a good reflection on the British character," he said.

Good-willed patriotism was also the tone taken by an organised group of Communist Party members from Beijing's huge Capital Iron and Steel Corp, posing for pictures on top of the ruins with a large scarlet hammer-and-sickle party flag.

"We are very happy about Hong Kong," said smelter official Zhao Cai -- although he admitted that on a sweltering Beijing summer morning he would not normally have chosen to travel far across town to ponder national pride.
Elsewhere in the capital, free time was the top topic for some employees granted a three-day break to mark the handover.
"Most of the people at my company are more interested in talking about what they will do on their days off than in Hong Kong itself," said one worker at a Sino-Japanese joint-venture.
Those involved in Beijing's vigorous private sector appeared least impressed by the deluge of official propaganda that has surrounded preparations for Hong Kong's return.
Authorities anxious to spruce up the city before the handover ordered the demolition of a row of small kiosks near one international hotel, local stallholders said.

The move had hit business hard and local merchants could not understand the connection between their business and matters of national sovereignty, said one carpet seller forced to hawk his wares from a tiny shop set further back from the busy road.
"They knocked down the stalls because of the return of Hong Kong," he said. "Who can ever tell what the government is thinking?"
